text.p: Edward Said leans forward in his leather armchair to launch another verbal dart at Yasser Arafat.
"Arafat's regime is as bad if not worse than the occupation," he begins from his jumbled study at New York's Columbia University.

Arafat is an autocrat. A lousy negotiator, the English and comparative literature professor says, warming to his theme. The Israelis run rings around the PLO leader, violate Palestinian rights and get the world to applaud them. The Oslo self-rule accord is a sell-out.

Such criticism would bring a midnight knock on the door from Arafat's police if made in the West Bank or Gaza. Said, a Palestinian who has been in the United States since he was 15, knows it. That is why he is nervous about going back.
In books and articles he has been a relentless critic of the 1993 Israeli-PLO agreement on interim Palestinian autonomy.
He is a constant thorn in Arafat's flesh that some have tried to remove.

"There's a written order from the Ministry of Information to confiscate my books," Said said. Arabic translations of Said's works disappeared from the West Bank four months ago but Arafat's Palestinian Authority denied banning his books.

"That is not true," says Said. His books are banned and he has been denounced on Palestinian radio, he asserts. He visited his son in the West Bank this summer but he wonders whether it would be safe to return.
"I am cautious. I still regard it as my homeland and believe it is my right to go there but if they are so over-zealous about the books how will they behave towards the author?" he asked.

Said is scathing in his assessment of the leadership skills of Arafat and his PLO colleagues. He believes the U.S.-driven Middle East peace process in general, and Oslo in particular, is flawed and favours Israel.
"I would never have trusted the Americans nor the Norwegians," he said of the Oslo mediators. "The Norwegian Labour Party has been in cahoots with the Mossad and Zionists for 40 years."

He said Arafat had not realised what he was getting into. PLO negotiators were ill-prepared and lacked expertise. The Israelis always came to the negotiating table with a battery of lawyers and map-makers.

Arafat thought partial self-rule would translate into statehood but that was unlikely under an Israeli Labour government, even less likely under the present conservative Likud administration, Said says.

"There is a gradual realisation among Palestinians that Oslo is the final status...The encroachment of settlements and roads means that we are living in Bantustans," Said argues. "We are lost. There is a sense that neither Israel nor the Arabs are delivering "
Meanwhile, Arafat tries to stifle debate about how the Palestinians should proceed by muzzling the media and turning the elected Legislative Council into a rubber stamp, he says.
"Democracy is being postponed. What bothers me is the complete silence. Worse there is a group of Palestinian policy experts who says it's inappropriate to talk of democracy."
Said says he has severed ties with Arafat and his colleagues. "I have no contact with the Palestinian Authority, I feel that so many of them are mediocrities, incompetents and liars."
He says Arafat has no concept of how to run a modern state and does not understand the workings of the American political system, unlike Jewish groups.
"Arafat is unreformable, his method of governing is so flawed, corrupt. It is not up to the task," Said concludes.
He knows that such armchair criticism riles those who thought Oslo was the only way to secure Middle East peace.
Charging for the moral high ground he rejects the whole process because it denies justice to all Palestinians by ignoring the Diaspora, those dispossessed by Israel's creation in 1948.
He says he favours a negotiated peace and Palestinian state alongside Israel but he has a different route map to his goal.

"What we have is the power of refusal. We need a new peace," Said says. He wants to harness the Palestinian community outside the West Bank and Gaza to reform the PLO, which is still based in Tunis, and to use their skill and energies in dealings with Israel.
"I'd certainly make more use of the exile community.
"We need more outside input in revitalising the PLO and ...more involvement in the final status talks."
As for his own role he believes he has to continue to show Palestinians an alternative path and to make Israel face up to its responsibility for the Palestinians' plight since 1948.
"Palestinians haven't tried to reach the Israeli mind in the way blacks did to white South Africans, to make them confront their history."
"The role of intellectuals now is to address Israel in stern terms about its past," Said added.
